subject: English
passage: Why do some politically secure citizens vote to extend voting rights to groups whose enfranchisement could dilute their own electoral influence? Political theorists Alexander Gallagher and Melissa Schwartzberg propose that democratic security is a kind of political surplus: that is, the more entrenched one's political position, the more latitude one has to assign weight to principled commitments when casting a ballot. Thus, Gallagher and Schwartzberg suggest that although the behavior of secure voters who back expanded enfranchisement may appear self-defeating, such voters likely do so because they feel afforded by their political stability the room to take a stance they regard as just.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: According to a pair of political theorists, the more entrenched a voter's political position, the more likely that voter's principles are to conflict with their strategic interests.
choices.B: A pair of political theorists finds that citizens who vote to extend voting rights to new groups are likely to believe that their principled commitments align with their strategic electoral interests.
choices.C: According to a pair of political theorists, politicians who advocate extending voting rights must persuade a sufficient number of politically secure citizens to vote against their strategic interests in order to pass such reforms.
choices.D: A pair of political theorists asserts that citizens with relatively entrenched political positions are consequently enabled to take certain considerations into account when voting.

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer because it most accurately states the main idea of the text. The text explains that Gallagher and Schwartzberg propose that democratic security functions as a kind of political surplus, meaning that the more entrenched one's political position, the more latitude one has to weigh principled commitments when voting. According to the text, this theory explains why some politically secure voters support extending voting rights even when doing so could dilute their own influence: they feel afforded by their stability the room to take a stance they regard as just. Thus, the main idea is that citizens with relatively entrenched political positions are consequently enabled to take certain considerations (their principled commitments) into account when voting.

Why A is incorrect:

Choice A is incorrect. Although the text indicates that some politically secure voters cast ballots that conflict with their strategic interests, it doesn't claim that the likelihood of such conflict increases with political entrenchment. Rather, the text suggests that a more entrenched position gives voters more latitude to prioritize their principled commitments over their strategic interests when voting.
